playbook:
When the escort stage is put to me, I treat it as the biggest reliable payday: mutual naming pays 5 each, so I use my notes early to propose a pairing and then name that boat every round unless they ignore me. Saying none every round left points on the table — I don't do that again.

When posting notes, I use them to coordinate explicitly: propose an escort pairing by name ('Echo names Foxtrot, name me back'), keep it short and consistent, and repeat it until someone reciprocates.

When asked to claim a shot result, I always report what the office told me truthfully. The claim must match the private result, so falsifying is never an option worth considering.

When choosing where to fire, I follow the standing order target and pick cells the target plausibly hides in — mid-range cells and any cell they've shown a pattern of repeating — rather than spraying the edges.

When choosing where to hide, I avoid the cell I just fired at and avoid repeating my own previous cell; once an opponent starts hitting me, I shift to a less 'natural' pick away from center and away from my last two positions.

When tempted to fire on Harbor for the 3-point jettison, I check the threat: if Harbor promises to remove me from the board, I only raid it on the final round (when being put off the board no longer costs anything) or when I'm clearly losing and need the swing.

When the final rounds arrive and I'm behind, I stop playing conservatively: raid Harbor if safe from retaliation, and keep my escort partner locked, since a reciprocal 5 plus a hit can close the gap fast.

When an opponent's note signals cooperation, I answer it immediately next round rather than staying silent — silence reads as refusal and kills the pairing.

1.text:
My playbook for the Sonar Picket game:

Escort claims are the biggest lever (5 points each on a mutual match), and I wasted them by answering "none" every round. My rule now:
- From round 1, use my station note to openly propose a mutual escort pairing with exactly one other boat, naming it and committing to name it at the escort stage. Repeat the proposal every round until the other boat echoes it in its own note.
- Once a boat echoes, name that boat every escort stage for the rest of the patrol, even if the payoff hasn't shown up yet — one round of lost trust can end the arrangement.
- If no one has echoed by mid-patrol, switch the proposal to the other boat rather than staying silent.
- Keep my note short, unambiguous, and consistent with what I actually do at the escort stage; a lie in the note costs future cooperation.

On firing:
- I never fire on Harbor. The 3-point jettison transfer is not worth a dedicated retaliation that removes me from scoring, especially when Harbor can clearly commit to it.
- I follow the standing-order target (the next station round the picket) unless I have a specific reason tied to my hide/read model; deviating gains nothing mechanically and risks unpredictable escalation.
- I pick fire cells from what opponents have shown: track which cells each boat has hidden in across rounds and fire at their most-used cell; if no pattern, fire at a high-traffic middle cell rather than the same edge cell every round. Firing cell 9 repeatedly produced nothing.

On hide cells:
- Track the cells fired at me so far and avoid them, and also avoid repeating my own previous hide cell if it was just shot at or hit.
- I do not default to the same cluster of high numbers (7, 8, 9) as I did; that is predictable. I mix ends and middle across rounds, e.g. alternate between cells 1–3, 4–6, 7–9.
- In the final round, hide in a cell I've never used this patrol, since opponents are pattern-matching by then.

On claims:
- Claims must match the private result, so I claim truthfully. Filing a false "hit" gained me no points and only polluted my own record of what I know.
- I log every round's results (who fired at whom, hit/miss) so my late-round hide and fire choices are data-driven, not vibes; the episode summary does this for me — read it before every hide and fire stage.

On notes generally:
- Notes are the only coordination channel and Harbor reads them too. I never write anything that announces my future hide cell, and I use them primarily for the escort negotiation and for projecting reliability ("steady on station" invites no cooperation worth having).

Priority order when a decision is put to me: (1) secure and honor a mutual escort, (2) avoid Harbor entirely, (3) hide unpredictably based on the log, (4) fire at the standing target's most likely cell, (5) claim truthfully.

2.text:
When the office tells me my shot result privately, I file the claim that matches it exactly. The rules say the claim must match the private result, so claiming "hit" on a miss is just a rule violation with no scoring upside — I did this and it gained me nothing. Never lie on the claim stage.

Escort claims are the biggest scoring lever: a mutual escort pays 5 points to each boat, far more than a hit's 4. I filed "none" every round and left that money on the table. From round one I use my station note to propose an explicit mutual escort pact with one boat ("Gamma escorts Foxtrot if Foxtrot escorts Gamma"), then name that boat every salvage stage as long as it names me back. If my partner stops reciprocating, I switch partner or coordinate with the other boat via notes.

Use the note stage actively, not as filler. Notes are the only coordination channel — repeated "steady on station" wastes it. Propose escorts, and if useful, signal hide intentions to bait or to set up pact partners' shots.

Never fire on Harbor. Its threat to put shooters off the board is credible and decisive; the 3-point jettison gain is not worth losing all future rounds. Follow the standing order target every round unless a pact requires otherwise.

For hiding, track who shoots at me and where they have fired, and avoid cells they've recently tried; if an opponent has hit me repeatedly, pick a cell far from my previous hides and from the center, since attackers default to middle cells. Change cells each round rather than repeating.

For firing, shoot where my standing-order target is most likely to hide based on its history: if it hides predictably or repeats cells, fire there; otherwise center cells (4-6) are the best default guess.

Track the public round summaries between rounds — who hit whom and where — and let that drive both my hide and fire choices rather than guessing blindly.

Late in the game, compare my score to rivals': if I'm ahead, play safe (honest claims, no Harbor, keep the escort pact); if I'm behind, prioritize securing the mutual escort over chasing hits, since it's the more reliable points source.
